MODEL INTERPRETATION

Baseline Logistic Regression performed best among the tested models

The baseline model recorded the strongest accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score and ROC-AUC among the three evaluated alternatives. Threshold selection should still consider campaign costs, the value of retained customers and the effectiveness of retention actions. ACTION PRIORITIES
MEASUREMENT AND FOLLOW-UP

Evaluate retention actions using measurable outcomes

Track customer retention, churn rate, campaign response and the number of customers successfully retained. Compare outcomes with an appropriate control group where possible. Do not assume that a customer who receives an offer has been retained because of it.

DECISION BRIEF • BASELINE COHORT: 7,043 CUSTOMERS

Churn risk is concentrated — retention effort should be targeted, early and measurable.

Prioritise customers showing multiple risk signals, investigate the experience behind those signals, and test interventions before scaling them.

01HIGHEST PRIORITY

Early-tenure Fiber customers on month-to-month contracts

WHAT HAPPENED

The highest-risk combination contains 440 customers; 332 churned. Its 75.45% churn rate is 48.91 percentage points above the overall rate.

WHY IT MAY BE HAPPENING

Short tenure and low contract commitment coincide with Fiber service. Setup friction, reliability concerns or first-bill confusion are hypotheses, not proven causes in this dataset.

WHAT TO DO

  1. Build a watchlist for Month-to-month + 0–6 Months + Fiber optic + Electronic Check.
  2. Review installation, first-bill clarity and service faults; contact customers with a relevant resolution before offering discounts.

Measure: 30/60/90-day retention, issue resolution and holdout-group uplift.

02HIGH PRIORITY

Contract commitment is strongly associated with churn

WHAT HAPPENED

Observed churn is 42.71% for month-to-month customers, compared with 11.27% for one-year and 2.83% for two-year contracts.

WHY IT MAY BE HAPPENING

Month-to-month customers have fewer contractual barriers to leaving. Contract type may also reflect customer needs or prior experience; this comparison does not prove that contract length causes retention.

WHAT TO DO

  1. Offer a transparent one-year option at appropriate renewal or service-review moments.
  2. Explain the value, total cost, flexibility and cancellation terms; never pressure customers into a longer commitment.

Measure: Voluntary conversion, 90-day churn, complaints and retention versus a comparable holdout.

03HIGH PRIORITY

The first six months are the most vulnerable period

WHAT HAPPENED

Customers with 0–6 months'' tenure have a 52.94% churn rate. The rate declines across longer tenure bands, reaching 9.51% at 49–72 months.

WHY IT MAY BE HAPPENING

New customers have had less time to build loyalty and may still be evaluating whether the service meets expectations. The dataset does not identify individual cancellation reasons.

WHAT TO DO

  1. Introduce a structured 14-, 30- and 60-day onboarding check-in.
  2. Ask about setup, service quality and billing; route unresolved issues to support with clear ownership.

Measure: Onboarding completion, early-life complaints and 90-day retention.

04TEST OPPORTUNITY

Support and security add-ons identify customers with different risk profiles

WHAT HAPPENED

Churn is higher among customers without Tech Support (41.64%) and without Online Security (41.77%) than among customers with those services.

WHY IT MAY BE HAPPENING

Add-on ownership may reflect different customer needs, tenure or engagement. The observed association does not establish that purchasing an add-on will prevent churn.

WHAT TO DO

  1. Offer a needs-based service review and explain relevant support or security options.
  2. Test voluntary add-on education against a holdout; disclose price and terms clearly.

Measure: Adoption, complaints and retention uplift versus holdout.

05MODEL-LED PRIORITY

A 0.50 model threshold misses many churners

WHAT HAPPENED

At 0.50, the baseline model identifies 209 of 374 churners (55.88%) and misses 165. At 0.30, it identifies 282 of 374 (75.40%) but flags more customers.

WHY IT MATTERS

A lower threshold captures more potential churners but increases review workload and false positives. The best threshold depends on capacity, intervention cost and incremental retention value.

WHAT TO DO

  1. Evaluate 0.30 as a pilot threshold, not an approved production rule.
  2. Use low-cost checks first; validate calibration, later-period performance and subgroup fairness before deployment.

Measure: Churn capture, contact-to-save conversion and cost per incremental save.

06RECOMMENDED EXECUTION

Turn the findings into a controlled 90-day retention pilot

WEEK 1Build the cohort

Identify eligible customers, confirm contact permissions and establish a baseline.

WEEKS 2–3Diagnose and contact

Review service, billing and onboarding issues; record reasons and outcomes.

WEEKS 4–8Test interventions

Compare targeted support and relevant offers with business-as-usual holdouts.

DAY 90Evaluate impact

Scale only actions that show incremental retention and acceptable cost.

DECISION RULE

Judge success by incremental customers retained, customer experience and cost — not by the number of messages sent or offers accepted.

Analytical guardrail: These are historical observational patterns, not proof of causality or current customer risk. Campaign profitability, customer lifetime value and intervention effectiveness still require testing and additional data.
